# Introduction

## Motivation

All domains of biology involve relational information, such as links between
genes, organisms, and their interactions. For example, organisms form symbiotic
or antagonistic relationships, consume specific foods, or avoid others, creating
a web of connections that define biological systems. When this relational
information is systematically organised and made accessible through databases
such as UniProt (proteins), Rhea (reactions), and KEGG (metabolic pathways), it
empowers scientists to build upon decades of research. However, leveraging
these resources in routine bioinformatic analyses is often hindered by
challenges such as inaccessible data repositories, incompatible formats, and
the sheer volume of data that exceeds local storage capacities. Without a
structured approach, navigating the labyrinth of biological knowledge can feel
overwhelming, time-consuming, and discouraging.

With its reproducible graph of interlinked biological resources and a robust
toolkit to explore it, ariadne is designed to simplify this process by
"Assembling Relational Information Across the Database Network". ariadne can be
used for knowledge-driven annotation, feature stratification, and goal-oriented
selection. For instance, it enables functional annotation of microbial features
using databases like ChocoPhlAn and WoL, or stratification by Gut Modules and
Bug Signatures. ariadne also extends to other biological data types, such as
metabolites, proteins, or genes, making it a flexible tool for integrating
relational knowledge into routine bioinformatic analyses (example use cases are
presented in
[this vignette](https://minotau-r.github.io/ariadne/articles/use_cases.html)).

# Tutorial

This tutorial showcases the programmatic usage of ariadne in R/RStudio. For the Python extension, check [ariadnePy](https://github.com/Minotau-R/ariadnePy). For
the Shiny app, check [ariadneApp](https://github.com/Minotau-R/ariadneApp).

## Installation

The Bioconductor release version can be installed as follows:

```{r install-release, eval = FALSE}
if( !requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE) ){
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("ariadne")
```

For the latest functionality, the devel version can be installed as follows:

```{r install-beta, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

# Initialise devel version
BiocManager::install(version = "devel")

BiocManager::install("ariadne")
```

## Import and explore the resource graph

ariadne combines different resources into a single graph highlighting the links
between biological entities. The way that ariadne retrieves and combines
relational data is further described in
[this vignette](https://minotau-r.github.io/ariadne/articles/resources.html).
In a nutshell, the data package ariadneDB contains information about the feature
types and mappings across a handful of popular databases, represented as graphs
and stored in Zenodo.

```{r lib, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ariadne)
library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(DT)
```

The resource graph can be imported with the function `ariadne`, which returns
the combined resources as a single igraph object.

```{r fetch}
# Import resource graph
graph <- ariadne()
```

The graph can also be visualised with `plotPath`.

```{r plot}
# Plot resource graph
plotPath(graph)
```

Let's say we need to find the links between gene functions and enzyme activity
represented by KEGG orthologues (ko) and enzyme commission ids (ec),
respectively. The function `searchPath` can be used to find the `k` shortest
paths in the graph.

```{r search}
# Search for paths from ko to ec
searchPath(graph, ko ~ ec, k = 3)
```

The top three paths found include the KEGG direct ko-ec link and the paths
through uniref90 or uniref50 provided by ChocoPhlAn in combination with UniProt.
Assuming that we are interested in the latter, paths satisfying specific
requirements can be selected with the arguments `include`, `exclude` and
`res.name`.

```{r plot-path}
plotPath(graph, ko ~ ec, include = "uniref90", prune = TRUE)
```

In addition, the graph can be explored using all native functions from the
igraph package. For example, we can sort its nodes by degree, that is, the
number of adjacent edges:

```{r degree}
# Find and sort node degrees
node_degrees <- graph |>
    degree(mode = "all") |>
    sort(decreasing = TRUE)

# Select nodes above degree threshold
node_degrees <- node_degrees[node_degrees >= 10]

# View node degrees
kable(node_degrees, col.names = "degree")
```

We can also list all the nodes in the neighbourhood of a certain node:

```{r neighbour}
# List neighbours of ko node
neighbors(graph, "ko", mode = "all")
```

## Select and customise the resource graph

The available resources default to the latest version found in the original
database.

```{r res-defaults}
# List available resource versions
versions <- listResourceVersions(default = TRUE)

# View versions
datatable(versions)
```

Some resources have multiple versions, which can be selected through the
argument `versions`. 

```{r res-versions}
# List custom versions
versions <- list(BugSigDB = "v1.2.2", WoL = "v20April2021")

# Import graph with custom versions
graph <- ariadne(versions = versions)
```

If the resource you need is missing, but you know where its mapping files
reside (also locally in your machine), it is possible to add it as a custom
resource to the ariadne graph using the function `addResource`. For example,
we can add the links between taxa and antibiotic resistance traits from the EMBL
AMR Portal.

```{r}
# Set URL to custom resource
url <- "https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/amr_portal/releases/2025-12/"
url <- paste0(url, "genotype.csv.gz")

# Add resource to ariadne graph
graph <- addResource(
    graph,
    url,
    res.name = "AMR",
    select = c("taxon_id", "antibiotic_ontology"),
    col.names = c("taxid", "aro")
)

# Search for newly added path
searchPath(graph, taxid ~ aro)
```

## Cross the graph to link biological entities

We decide to go through the simplest path, which corresponds to a `k` of 1. The
links between KO and EC are found by the function `weavePath`, which fetches
the necessary resources and weaves a path from ko to ec.

```{r}
# Weave path from ko to ec
ko2ec <- weavePath(graph, ko ~ ec, k = 1)
```

The links are provided as a **linkmap**, a 2-column table where each row is a
pair of ids (one ko and one ec). When available, the feature names are returned
as a third optional column.

```{r}
# View some links
datatable(ko2ec)
```

The weave can be initialised with a set of identifiers belonging to the `from`
id type. This is specified with the argument `init`.

```{r}
# Define custom ko initial values
ko.ids <- c("K00665", "K05913", "K11533")

# Weave path with initial values
ko2ec <- weavePath(graph, ko ~ ec, init = ko.ids)

# View links
knitr::kable(ko2ec)
```

Sometimes, we would like to know how much each origin id covers each target id
in terms of percent coverage (useful for pathway enrichment analysis). This can
be achieved with the alternative function `weaveComplex`. For example, we can
estimate the percentage of kegg pathways covered by different ec ids, and select
only those links above a certain `threshold`.

```{r}
# Find complex links between ko and kegg pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(
    graph,
    ec ~ kegg_path,
    threshold = 0.5
)

# View some links
knitr::kable(ec2path)
```

The links can be visualised with the function `plotModules`.

```{r}
# Visualise links
plotModules(ko2path, layout = "sugiyama") + coord_flip()
```

## Ensure reproducibility of the ariadne workflow

A path table is a metadata describing the complete workflow. The data object
`pathMeta` shows an example of the contained information and format.

```{r pathMeta}
# Import pathMeta object
data("pathMeta", package = "ariadne")

# View pathMeta object
datatable(pathMeta)
```

To generate a the table for a given path, `drawPath` can be used.

```{r draw}
# Draw path table from ko to ec
path_df <- drawPath(graph, ko ~ ec, k = 1)

datatable(path_df)
```

The returned path can be directly passed to `weavePath` to reproduce the full
ariadne workflow.

```{r weave-drawn}
ko2ec.simple <- weavePath(path_df)

datatable(ko2ec.simple)
```

Similarly, the path table can also be passed to `weaveComplex` to reproduce a
coverage-based ariadne workflow.

```{r complex-drawn}
ko2ec.complex <- weaveComplex(path_df)

datatable(ko2ec.complex)
```

## Add results to SummarizedExperiment for downstream analyses

ariadne works in combination with the wider Bioconductor framework, in
particular the data containers derived from SummarizedExperiment (SE), the mia
package for microbiome data analysis, and the anansi package for
knowledge-driven association analysis. First, we import the `Tengeler2020`
TreeSE object.

```{r}
# Import experiment object
data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")

# Rename experiment object
tse <- Tengeler2020

# View experiment object
tse
```

We also import `butyrate` linkmap on butyrate-producing bacteria, which is
included in the ariadne package as an example output of the `weave*` functions.

```{r}
# Import butyrate linkmap
data("butyrate", package = "ariadne")

# View butyrate linkmap
datatable(butyrate)
```

The function `getModules` matches each level of the origin feature type
(taxname in this case) with any variable specified in `key` (in the given order)
and it returns a modules table where rows and columns represent origin and
target features, respectively, and cell values indicate presence/absence
membership or coverage fraction.

```{r}
# Get butyrate-producer module membership
modules <- getModules(tse, butyrate, key = c("Genus", "Family"))

# View modules table
datatable(modules)
```

Using the function `addModules`, the modules table is directly added to the
side information of the TreeSE object, so that it can be used in downstream
analysis.

```{r}
# Add modules to experiment as names instead of ids
tse <- addModules(tse, butyrate, key = "Genus", as = "names")
```

The mia package provides two key methods to apply module-wise operations to
a SE object. The first is `agglomerateByModule`, which agglomerates the count
table along `by` for each module in the side information included in `group`
(only one in this case).

```{r}
# Agglomerate features by membership to butyrate-producer module
mod.se <- agglomerateByModule(tse, by = "rows", group = "butyrate")

# Plot abundance of butyrate producers
plotAbundance(mod.se)
```

The second method allows to apply any operation module-wise on an SE object
using the functio `applyByModule`. For example, it is possible to estimate
alpha diversity for each module (only one in this case), which is sometimes
called _functional diversity_.

```{r}
# Estimate alpha diversity for each module
tse <- applyByModule(
    tse,
    .by = "rows",
    .group = "butyrate",
    FUN = getAlpha,
    index = c("shannon", "faith"),
    min.group.size = 2
)

# viz functional alpha/beta
plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "shannon_1")
```
